strengths: The joint Brownian-bridge likelihood and closed-form covariance estimator provide an explicit statistical foundation for extending BBScore. A document-level score that supports comparisons across texts is relevant to NLP evaluation.

The reported shuffle results are promising. With GPT-2, BBScoreV2 reaches 98.17% versus Unified Coherence’s 96.09% for block size 10, and 94.78% on mixed shuffling with block size 1. Table 2 also reports substantial improvements over BBScore in transfer between datasets.

The experiments examine several block sizes, language-model backbones, alternative training objectives, and human–AI comparisons. The mathematical appendix and acknowledged limitations improve transparency.
weaknesses: The advertised length invariance does not follow from Equation 5. For the stated integer-time Brownian bridge, det(Σ_T)=1/T, so normalization leaves log(T)/(2(T−1)) in the score and its expectation under the assumed model. Thus even correctly modeled sequences have length-dependent expected scores. This does not invalidate the shuffle gains, but it undermines a central theoretical claim; corrected calibration or narrower claims and length-controlled experiments are needed.

Important reproduction and evaluation details remain unspecified. Appendix A.2 describes the alternative SP encoder, whereas the main CL encoder’s latent dimension, training configuration, and contextual sentence-encoding procedure are unclear. The manuscript also does not adequately specify HC3 sample counts, covariance-fitting versus evaluation splits, or whether detection accuracy measures pairwise ranking or thresholded classification. The reference to submitted configurations cannot resolve these questions from the supplied manuscript.

The representation analysis overstates what its evidence establishes. Absence of temporal structure in two principal components does not demonstrate its absence from raw embeddings; Figure 2 also compares token embeddings with sentence representations. Likewise, worse performance from alternative training losses does not establish independence across latent dimensions. Matched sentence-level probes and fixed-encoder comparisons using identity, diagonal, and full covariance would better test the claimed mechanisms.

The evidence supports artificial shuffle discrimination more clearly than general coherence or domain-independent textual dynamics. WikiText and WikiSection both contain Wikipedia articles; low document overlap does not establish a substantial distribution shift. Appendix D identifies overlapping documents without reporting their removal. Human-rated coherence and transfer across substantially different genres remain untested, although the paper appropriately acknowledges the human-evaluation limitation.

Comparative conclusions need qualification. Table 1 provides no Unified Coherence result for mixed shuffling despite claims of superiority on that task, and smaller improvements lack uncertainty estimates. AI-detection evidence is restricted to HC3: DetectGPT with ten perturbations substantially exceeds BBScoreV2, as the authors acknowledge. The demonstrated advantage is therefore a restricted inference-budget tradeoff whose practical value needs clearer evaluation.

The computational argument in Section 5.5 is incorrect: quadratic dependence on sequence length is not fundamental to this score. The Brownian-bridge temporal precision matrix is tridiagonal, permitting linear dependence on length for fixed latent dimension and precomputed structural precision. Furthermore, score-computation timing and inference counts do not establish end-to-end efficiency. Together with the normalization and evaluation-protocol issues, these concerns require revision before a sound, reproducible Findings recommendation.
